blocks.title: 1. How many zeros does a polynomial have?
teacherCues: Ask: "How many solutions does x² = 4 have? What about x² = –4?" Then discuss that complex numbers make every polynomial have a complete set of solutions.
Write f(x) = (x–1)²(x+2)³ and ask: "How many zeros? How many distinct?"

discoveryHook.scenario: Every polynomial of degree n can be broken down into exactly n linear factors—some real, some complex, some repeated. This guarantee, called the [[kw:Fundamental Theorem of Algebra]], tells us that we always have the right number of zeros, even if we can't see them on a graph.

explanation: The [[kw:Fundamental Theorem of Algebra]] says: Every polynomial of degree n ≥ 1 has at least one complex zero.
From this, the [[kw:Linear Factorization Theorem]] follows: A degree‑n polynomial can be written as $ f(x) = a_n (x - c_1)(x - c_2) \cdots (x - c_n) $, where each $c_i$ is a complex number.
This means a polynomial of degree n has exactly n zeros, counting multiplicity (repeated zeros count).
Zeros can be real or complex. Complex zeros with real coefficients always come in conjugate pairs (more on that later).

visuals.title: Counting zeros (real and complex, with multiplicities)

formulaCard.title: Linear Factorization
notes: Count of factors = degree = number of zeros.

examples.title: A – Count the zeros
examples.prompt: How many zeros does $ f(x)=x^4-1 $ have? List them.

examples.title: B – Repeated zero counts as two
examples.prompt: Explain why $ f(x) = (x-3)^2 $ has two zeros.
examples.peerPrompt: Talk to a partner: If you solve (x-3)² = 0, how many solutions do you get? Does the graph cross the axis?
steps: The equation (x-3)² = 0 gives x = 3 (a double root).
The factorization has (x-3) twice → zero of multiplicity 2.
Graph touches and turns at x=3; it still counts as two zeros.

examples.title: C – Complex zeros also count
examples.prompt: State the number of zeros for $ f(x)=x^2+4 $ and identify them.

confusionCorner.title: Total zeros = degree, always
confusionCorner.body: Even if you can't see a zero on the graph (like a complex zero), it still exists. The Fundamental Theorem guarantees the exact number, counting multiplicities.

questions.prompt: A polynomial of degree 5 has exactly ___ zeros in the complex number system (counting multiplicities).
hints: The degree tells you how many.
Think of the Linear Factorization Theorem.

questions.prompt: How many distinct zeros does $ f(x)=(x+1)^3(x-2) $ have?
True or false: A cubic polynomial with real coefficients must have at least one real zero.
hints: Odd degree means you can't pair all zeros as complex.

blocks.title: 2. The Rational Zero Test — making a list
teacherCues: Write $ f(x)=2x^3+3x^2-8x+3 $ and ask: "What are all the possible fractions that could be zeros?"
Demonstrate listing factors of constant term over factors of leading coefficient.

discoveryHook.scenario: When factoring doesn't work, how do we find if a polynomial has a rational zero? The [[kw:Rational Zero Test]] gives us a short list of candidates — fractions formed from the factors of the constant term and the leading coefficient.

explanation: If a polynomial $ f(x)=a_n x^n + ... + a_0 $ has integer coefficients, any rational zero $ p/q $ (in lowest terms) must have:
- $ p $ = factor of the constant term $ a_0 $
- $ q $ = factor of the leading coefficient $ a_n $
So the possible rational zeros are: $ \pm \frac{\text{factors of } a_0}{\text{factors of } a_n} $.
This gives a list of candidates. You then test each one using synthetic division (or substitution).

visuals.title: Making the candidate list for $ f(x)=2x^3+3x^2-8x+3 $

formulaCard.title: Rational Zero Test
formulaCard.formula: $$ \text{Possible rational zeros: } \frac{\text{factors of } a_0}{\text{factors of } a_n} $$
notes: List includes both positive and negative.
It doesn't tell you which are actual zeros; you must test.

examples.title: A – Leading coefficient 1
examples.prompt: List the possible rational zeros of $ f(x)=x^3 + x + 1 $.
steps: Test: $ f(1)=3 $, $ f(‑1)=‑1 $. Neither zero → no rational zeros.

examples.title: B – Making a list for a non‑1 leading coefficient
examples.prompt: List all possible rational zeros of $ f(x)=3x^3-4x^2+2x-5 $.
examples.peerPrompt: With a partner, write down the factors of 5 and 3, then form all fractions. How many candidates do you get?

examples.title: C – Test some candidates
examples.prompt: For $ f(x)=x^4-x^3+x^2-3x-6 $, list possible rational zeros and find the actual ones.
steps: Test x=‑1: synthetic division gives remainder 0 → zero.
Quotient: $ x^3-2x^2+3x-6 $. Test x=2 on this: remainder 0 → zero.
Quotient $ x^2+3 $ has no real zeros. Rational zeros: –1, 2.

confusionCorner.title: Possible ≠ Actual
confusionCorner.body: The test only gives possibilities. Always test each candidate by plugging in or using synthetic division — otherwise you might miss the real answers.

questions.prompt: In the Rational Zero Test, p comes from factors of the ___ term.
List the possible rational zeros of $ f(x)=x^3-5x+2 $.
Is 1/2 a possible rational zero of $ f(x)=2x^3+5x-3 $? (yes/no)
hints: p: factors of –3 (±1,±3); q: factors of 2 (±1,±2).

blocks.title: 3. Smart searching: graphs + synthetic division
teacherCues: Show $ f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6 $ and ask: "We have 12 possible rational zeros. How can a graph reduce the work?"
Demonstrate synthetic division repeatedly to factor out found zeros.

discoveryHook.scenario: When the candidate list is long, you don't have to test blindly. A quick sketch or graphing tool shows where the curve crosses the x‑axis, and the [[kw:Intermediate Value Theorem]] helps locate zeros. Then synthetic division confirms them and reduces the polynomial for further searching.

explanation: Strategy to find zeros efficiently:
1. List all possible rational zeros (Rational Zero Test).
2. Use a graph (or a table of values) to estimate where the zeros might be. Focus on x‑intercepts near nice numbers.
3. Test the most promising candidates first (integers and simple fractions).
4. Once you find a zero, use synthetic division to divide the polynomial. The quotient has a lower degree, making it easier to find remaining zeros.
5. Repeat until the polynomial is fully factored.

rows.1: Try x=2 → synthetic div remainder 0 → zero

formulaCard.title: Zero‑finding loop
notes: Synthetic division confirms and reduces degree.
Remaining zeros are found from the reduced polynomial.

examples.title: A – Use a graph to find zeros
examples.prompt: Find all real zeros of $ f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6 $.

examples.title: B – Explain why the quotient helps
examples.prompt: Once you find one zero, why is it easier to find the remaining zeros?
examples.peerPrompt: Talk it through: After dividing by (x–2), the polynomial becomes a quadratic. How does that change the possible zeros list?
steps: Dividing by (x–2) reduces the degree from 3 to 2.
The new polynomial is $ 2x^2+5x-3 $, which can be factored or solved by quadratic formula.
No need for long candidate lists anymore.

examples.title: C – Apply the loop
examples.prompt: Find all real zeros of $ f(x)=x^4-x^3+x^2-3x-6 $ (same as earlier, but now use the loop).
steps: Test x=2 on quotient → zero, quotient $ x^2+3 $.
$ x^2+3=0 $ gives no real zeros. Real zeros: –1, 2.

confusionCorner.title: Graph estimates are not exact
confusionCorner.body: A graph may show a zero near 1.5, but the exact rational zero could be 3/2. Always verify with synthetic division to get the precise value.

questions.prompt: After finding that x=2 is a zero of a cubic, what degree is the quotient after synthetic division?
To narrow down a long list of possible rational zeros, use a ___ to see where the function crosses the x‑axis.
For $ f(x)=2x^3+x^2-13x+6 $, after synthetic division by x=2, the quotient is $ 2x^2+5x-3 $. Factor it.

blocks.title: 4. Complex zeros come in pairs
teacherCues: Ask: "If 2+3i is a zero of a polynomial with real coefficients, what else must be a zero?" Show the conjugate.
Illustrate building a polynomial from its zeros, using conjugate pairs.

discoveryHook.scenario: If a polynomial with real coefficients has a complex zero like 2+i, its conjugate 2–i is automatically a zero. This pairing makes complex zeros predictable and helps us construct polynomials from given zeros.

explanation: [[kw:Complex Conjugate Zeros Theorem]]: For a polynomial with real coefficients, if $ a+bi $ (b ≠ 0) is a zero, then $ a–bi $ is also a zero.
Complex zeros always appear in conjugate pairs.
A real‑coefficient polynomial of odd degree must have at least one real zero (because complex zeros come in twos).
When building a polynomial from given zeros, if a complex zero appears, you must include its conjugate.

formulaCard.title: Conjugate Pair Theorem
notes: An odd‑degree real polynomial must have at least one real zero.

examples.title: A – Find all zeros given one complex
examples.prompt: A cubic polynomial with real coefficients has zeros 2 and 3i. Find the third zero.
steps: Since 3i is a zero, its conjugate –3i must also be a zero.

examples.title: B – Why odd degree forces a real zero
examples.prompt: Explain why a cubic polynomial with real coefficients must have at least one real zero.
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss: If all three zeros were complex, could they be paired as conjugates?
steps: Complex zeros come in conjugate pairs (two at a time).
It's impossible to have three complex zeros without an unpaired one, so at least one must be real.

examples.title: C – Build a polynomial from zeros
examples.prompt: Find a 4th‑degree polynomial with real coefficients having zeros 1, 1, and 2–i.
steps: Multiply with $(x-1)^2 = x^2-2x+1$ to get $ x^4 - 6x^3 + 14x^2 - 14x + 5 $.

confusionCorner.title: Only for real coefficients!
confusionCorner.body: The conjugate pair rule applies only when the polynomial's coefficients are real. If any coefficient is not real, the conjugate may not be a zero.

questions.prompt: If 4 – i is a zero of a real‑coefficient polynomial, what other zero must it have?
hints: Change the sign of the imaginary part.

questions.prompt: A polynomial with real coefficients and degree 5 must have at least one real zero because complex zeros come in ___ pairs.
If a cubic polynomial has zeros 1 and i, what is the third zero?

blocks.title: 5. Blueprint Aid: Putting it all together
teacherCues: Walk through a full example: use Rational Zero Test, graph, synthetic division, then conjugate pairs to find all zeros (real and complex).
Emphasize the Understand → Solve → Conclude flow.

discoveryHook.scenario: Now we combine every tool: the Rational Zero Test, graph, synthetic division, and the Conjugate Pair Theorem. With this blueprint, you can tackle any polynomial zero‑finding problem step by step.

explanation: [[kw:Understand]]: Identify the polynomial's degree, leading coefficient, and constant term. List all possible rational zeros.

[[kw:Solve]]: Use a graph (or IVT) to estimate zeros. Test candidates with synthetic division. After finding one zero, divide and continue with the quotient. For complex zeros, remember they come in pairs.
[[kw:Conclude]]: Write the complete factorization with all zeros (real and complex), in standard form.

rows.1: Degree 3, leading coeff 1, constant -3. Possible rational zeros: ±1, ±3.
Graph suggests zero near 1. Test x=1: synthetic div → remainder 0. Quotient: $ x^2 - 4x + 3 = (x-1)(x-3) $.

visuals.title: Full blueprint with complex zeros: $ f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 2 $

rows.1: Test x=2 → zero. Quotient: $ x^2 + 1 $ → zeros: i, –i.

formulaCard.title: Zero‑Finding Blueprint
notes: 4. Complex zeros appear in conjugate pairs.

examples.title: A – All‑in‑one example
steps: Test x=2 → f(2)=0 → zero. Synthetic division gives quotient $ x^2+1 $.

examples.title: B – Explain the strategy
examples.prompt: Why do we use the Rational Zero Test first, then grapht, then synthetic division? Could we do it in a different order?
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss with a partner the pros and cons of each order.
steps: Rational Zero Test gives a complete list of possibilities.
Graph helps to pick likely candidates quickly.
Synthetic division confirms and reduces the polynomial for easier further solving.
The order is flexible but this sequence is efficient.

examples.title: C – Independent practice
examples.prompt: Find all zeros (real and complex) of $ f(x)=x^4-1 $.
steps: Test x=1 → zero, quotient $ x^3+x^2+x+1 $. Test x=–1 → zero, quotient $ x^2+1 $.

confusionCorner.title: Keep track of multiplicities
confusionCorner.body: When listing zeros, always note multiplicity. A zero of multiplicity 2 still counts as two zeros in the total count, even if the graph just touches.

questions.prompt: In the blueprint, after finding a zero, what is the next step?
When some zeros are complex, they always occur in ___ pairs.
hints: Two complex numbers that are mirrors.

questions.prompt: After finding that x=2 is a zero of $ f(x)=x^3-2x^2+x-2 $, what is the remaining quotient?
